name: African potato (Hypoxis hemerocallidea)
short: Lab: HIV-drug interactions possible. 1 possible intolerance in 24 with cancer (species unnamed). No significant efavirenz change in 10; no clinically significant liver/kidney change in 26 with HIV.
text: A review of herb and antiretroviral interactions reported that laboratory studies of several African traditional medicines, among which Hypoxis hemerocallidea showed some of the most complex effects, suggest possible interactions with HIV medicines through the drug-handling proteins CYP3A4, P-gp and PXR, and noted that only one clinical study (with efavirenz) had been done. In that study, in 10 healthy volunteers, a traditionally prepared African potato decoction taken daily for 14 days did not significantly alter the pharmacokinetics of a single dose of efavirenz; the abstract reports no adverse-event data. In an open-label 10-day pilot study in 26 adults with HIV in Zimbabwe taking a tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine and efavirenz regimen, African potato tablets (dosed by their hypoxoside content) taken by mouth produced no statistically significant change in liver tests and no change in creatinine, eGFR or electrolytes, while total protein rose and blood urea nitrogen fell; the authors concluded that this short-term exposure was not associated with clinically significant changes in liver or kidney function tests or electrolytes, and called for study of longer use in a larger population. In an older open study in 24 patients with lung cancer taking a standardised Hypoxis plant extract by mouth (the abstract does not name the species), no toxic effects attributable to hypoxoside were found and one episode of possible drug intolerance with anxiety, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea was noted. The human evidence is small and short-term.
